passages.where: At the high point of the first creation account the story breaks into poetry: God created humanity in his own image, male and female. Before anything is said about what people do, right or wrong, Scripture says what they are. That dignity was given, not earned, and sin has marred it without erasing it.

David marvels that God knit him together in his mother's womb and saw him before he was born. He praises God because he was made with care. The psalm does not say he was flawless; it says he was made by someone who knew him completely.

God speaks to Israel in exile, a people who had failed him and been sent away. He reminds them that he formed them, redeemed them and called them by name, and tells them they are precious and honored in his sight, and loved. The words are spoken to people who had every reason to think they had forfeited them.

David praises a God who does not deal with us as our sins deserve, and who removes them as far as the east is from the west. He compares God to a father with compassion for his children, who remembers that they are dust. God's knowledge of our weakness leads him to pity, not contempt.

John writes to believers whose own hearts sometimes condemn them. He does not tell them their hearts are always right. He says that God is greater than our hearts and knows all things, and that his verdict is the one that stands.

The Corinthians were busy ranking their teachers. Paul says he cares little about their verdict on him, and then adds that he does not even judge himself; the Lord is his judge. He refuses both the church's court and the court in his own head.

After the struggle of Romans 7, Paul gives the conclusion his whole letter has been building toward: there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. It is a law-court word. The verdict has been given, and it is not a reward for living well.

Paul distinguishes two kinds of sorrow. Godly sorrow turns toward God, leads to change, and ends in freedom that no one regrets. Worldly sorrow turns in on itself, goes round in circles, and brings death. Grief over sin is meant to lead somewhere, not to last forever.

Peter denies Jesus three times, and at the rooster's crow the Lord turns and looks at him. Only Luke records the look. Peter goes out and weeps bitterly. The scene ends in tears, but Jesus had already prayed that Peter's faith would not fail (Luke 22:32).

By a charcoal fire after the resurrection, Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him, one question for each denial. Each time he gives him work to do: feed my sheep. Jesus does not let Peter's worst night be the last word about him.

Zephaniah's book is full of judgment on a rebellious city. It ends with a song in which God is in the midst of his people, mighty to save, quieting them with his love and rejoicing over them with singing. The last word God speaks over them is delight.

misread.taken: “What a wretched man I am” is sometimes held up as the right way for a Christian to feel about himself, as if constant self-contempt were a sign of humility or holiness.
misread.says: The cry is real, and it is honest about the struggle between wanting the good and doing it. But it is not the end of the sentence. The answer comes at once as thanks: rescue is through Jesus Christ our Lord, and the next verse says there is now no condemnation for those in Christ. Christians differ on whether the “I” of these verses is a believer or a person under the law without the Spirit. On every reading, Paul does not stay in the cry, and the cry looks outside the self for rescue. Humility is not hatred of oneself; it is forgetting oneself in the presence of the God who rescues.

whole: If your self-hatred has turned into thoughts of hurting yourself, please tell someone today, and if you are in danger, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Self-hatred can sound like a constant voice: you are disgusting, you ruin everything, everyone would be better off without you, you will never change. Sometimes it grows from real failures and sins; sometimes from what others did or said, especially early in life; sometimes from comparison, illness or exhaustion; often from several at once. Christians can be especially vulnerable to it, because they take sin seriously and may have learned to treat self-contempt as a form of repentance.

The Bible takes sin more seriously than self-hatred does, and that is exactly why it refuses self-hatred as the answer. It begins with a dignity given before anything was done, the image of God, which sin has damaged but not erased. It names sin plainly and then deals with it outside us: a verdict given in Christ, no condemnation, a God greater than our hearts who knows everything and still calls his people precious. Self-hatred makes the self the judge and the sentence both. The gospel takes both roles away from us. Paul would not even judge himself; the Lord was his judge, and for those in Christ the Lord's verdict is no condemnation.

Peter is the Bible's clearest picture of this. He failed Jesus at the worst moment, wept bitterly, and could have spent his life defined by that night. Jesus met him by a fire and gave him three chances to say what he had once denied, and then gave him work to do. Godly sorrow leads somewhere; it turns toward God and ends in freedom. So the wisdom here is to bring the voice into the light. Tell someone what it says. Test its sentences against what God says. Confess real sin, and then believe the forgiveness, which is harder. Let others speak to you what you cannot yet say to yourself, and remember that the last word God speaks over his people is not contempt but delight.
sit: If someone you love spoke to themselves the way you speak to yourself, what would you say to them, and why do you think God would say less to you?

prayer.lead: Psalm 103 tells the soul what God is like before it asks for anything. Pray it slowly, as words spoken to you.

careLines.text: Feeling as if you are going under is not a sign that God has left you.
You do not have to pretend you are fine.
Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
